Question five. Why does select star cost more in a columnar warehouse? Because the scan follows the columns you name. The page's model: on a two hundred column table, three columns are one and a half percent of the data, if every column is the same width. Select star is all of it, and on per-byte billing you pay for every byte. Measured in DuckDB, on the million sales: select star read the whole nine point four megabyte file. Units by region, two columns, read under eight hundred kilobytes. It's bytes, not column count. Amount, random to the cent, is nearly half the file, so revenue by region read four point six megabytes. In a project, name the columns: a model built as a table from select star reads every column of its source on every build.

Question six. What is partitioning, and how does partition pruning save money? Partitioning splits a table into segments by a column, usually a date. A query that filters on that column reads only the matching segments, and skips the rest. That's pruning. The page's model: a year of data at two point four gigabytes a day. Unpartitioned, every query reads all eight hundred seventy-six gigabytes. Partitioned by day, a seven-day dashboard tile reads sixteen point eight: about fifty times less, and billed that way. In DuckDB, with the million sales in a folder per month, a query for March scans one file of twelve. Filter on region instead, and it reads all twelve: pruning only works on the partition column. And a query over all of history saves nothing, which is why the answer isn't to partition everything.
